claim: Chromatin accessibility is modulated in a variety of ways to create open and closed chromatin states, both of which are critical for eukaryotic gene regulation.
source: Chromatin accessibility is modulated in a variety of ways to create open and closed chromatin states, both of which are critical for eukaryotic gene regulation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about chromatin states and gene regulation.

claim: HS-AFM can track chromatin dynamics in real time.
source: By high-speed atomic force microscopy, we tracked chromatin dynamics in real time and determined the mean square displacement and diffusion constant for the variant centromeric CENP-A nucleosome.
evidence: The abstract states that the authors used HS-AFM to track chromatin dynamics and obtained specific measurements.

claim: The mean square displacement and diffusion constant for CENP-A nucleosomes can be determined by HS-AFM.
source: By high-speed atomic force microscopy, we tracked chromatin dynamics in real time and determined the mean square displacement and diffusion constant for the variant centromeric CENP-A nucleosome.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that these parameters were determined using HS-AFM.

claim: CENP-C reduces the diffusion constant and mobility of centromeric nucleosomes along the chromatin fiber.
source: Furthermore, we found that an essential kinetochore protein CENP-C reduces the diffusion constant and mobility of centromeric nucleosomes along the chromatin fiber.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the HS-AFM experiments.

claim: Overexpressing CENP-C results in reduced centromeric transcription.
source: Overexpressing CENP-C resulted in reduced centromeric transcription and impaired loading of new CENP-A molecules.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from in vivo experiments.

claim: Overexpressing CENP-C results in impaired loading of new CENP-A molecules.
source: Overexpressing CENP-C resulted in reduced centromeric transcription and impaired loading of new CENP-A molecules.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from in vivo experiments.

claim: Factors altering nucleosome mobility in vitro also correspondingly alter transcription in vivo.
source: From these data, we speculate that factors altering nucleosome mobility in vitro, also correspondingly alter transcription in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly presents this as speculation based on the data.

claim: Variant nucleosomes encode their own diffusion kinetics and mobility.
source: Subsequently, we propose a model in which variant nucleosomes encode their own diffusion kinetics and mobility, and where binding partners can suppress or enhance nucleosome mobility.
evidence: The abstract proposes this as part of a model based on the findings.

claim: Binding partners can suppress or enhance nucleosome mobility.
source: Subsequently, we propose a model in which variant nucleosomes encode their own diffusion kinetics and mobility, and where binding partners can suppress or enhance nucleosome mobility.
evidence: The abstract proposes this as part of a model based on the findings.

claim: More physically accessible chromatin is more transcriptionally permissive.
source: Decades of data strongly suggest that more physically accessible chromatin is also more transcriptionally permissive (Klemm et al., 2019; Maeshima et al., 2019 landmark papers from Weintraub and Groudine, 1976; Wu et al., 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Compacted chromatin or heterochromatin has been correlated with transcriptional restriction.
source: In contrast, compacted chromatin or heterochromatin has been correlated with transcriptional restriction (Allshire and Madhani, 2018; Flamm et al., 1969; Janssen et al., 2018; Schultz, 1936).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HP1 binds to H3K9me2/3 nucleosomes.
source: For instance, HP1 binds to H3K9me2/3 nucleosomes (Bannister et al., 2001; Nakayama et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Sanulli et al., 2019), ultimately resulting in transcriptionally repressive chromatin (Bannister et al., 2001; Escobar et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2001; Nakayama et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HP1 binding to H3K9me3 nucleosomes results in transcriptionally repressive chromatin.
source: For instance, HP1 binds to H3K9me2/3 nucleosomes (Bannister et al., 2001; Nakayama et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Sanulli et al., 2019), ultimately resulting in transcriptionally repressive chromatin (Bannister et al., 2001; Escobar et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2001; Nakayama et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon binding of HP1 to H3K9me3 nucleosomes, these nucleosomes' internal residues become more exposed to hydrogen/deuterium exchange.
source: Interestingly, upon binding of HP1 to H3K9me3 nucleosomes, these nucleosomes' internal residues become more exposed to hydrogen/deuterium exchange (Sanulli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Chromatin-binding proteins not only serve as a recruitment platform for other binding proteins but can rapidly alter the physical properties of individual nucleosomes.
source: This seminal finding suggests that chromatin-binding proteins not only serve as a recruitment platform for other binding proteins but can rapidly alter the physical properties of individual nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited finding about HP1 and H3K9me3 nucleosomes.

claim: HS-AFM has the capability to span the gap between optical/magnetic tweezers and single molecule tracking in cells.
source: However, a gap exists connecting these two technical approaches, namely assessing, and quantifying the dynamics of individual nucleosomes and correlating them with global chromatin dynamics. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) has the capability to span this gap.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of HS-AFM as a technique.

claim: HS-AFM permits real time tracking of single molecules in the context of interacting macromolecular complexes.
source: It is an in vitro based technique that permits real time tracking of single molecules in the context of interacting macromolecular complexes (e.g. myosin tracking on actin filaments, Ando, 2018; chromatin techniques reviewed in Melters and Dalal, 2021).
evidence: This statement describes the capabilities of HS-AFM and is supported by citations.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes recruit several centromeric proteins including CENP-C.
source: CENP-A nucleosomes recruit several centromeric proteins (Walstein et al., 2021; Mendiburo et al., 2011; Régnier et al., 2005), including CENP-C.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C functions as the blueprint for the formation of the kinetochore.
source: CENP-C in turn functions as the blueprint for the formation of the kinetochore (Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca and Musacchio, 2012; Hara et al., 2023; Walstein et al., 2021; Przewloka et al., 2007; Weir et al., 2016; Yatskevich et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The central domain of CENP-C (CENP-CCD) induces loss of CENP-A nucleosomal elasticity in silico and in vitro.
source: Recently, we reported that the central domain of CENP-C (CENP-CCD) induces loss of CENP-A nucleosomal elasticity in silico and in vitro (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding by the authors.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes show decreased hydrogen/deuterium exchange when bound by CENP-CCD.
source: This finding correlates with decreased hydrogen/deuterium exchange of CENP-A nucleosomes when bound by CENP-CCD (Falk et al., 2016; Falk et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C knock-down resulted in downregulation of centromeric transcription.
source: Interestingly, CENP-C knock-down resulted in downregulation of centromeric transcription (Bury et al., 2020), whereas CENP-C overexpression resulted in reduced RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) levels at the centromere and clustering of centromeric chromatin (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C overexpression resulted in reduced RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) levels at the centromere.
source: Interestingly, CENP-C knock-down resulted in downregulation of centromeric transcription (Bury et al., 2020), whereas CENP-C overexpression resulted in reduced RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) levels at the centromere and clustering of centromeric chromatin (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C overexpression resulted in clustering of centromeric chromatin.
source: Interestingly, CENP-C knock-down resulted in downregulation of centromeric transcription (Bury et al., 2020), whereas CENP-C overexpression resulted in reduced RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) levels at the centromere and clustering of centromeric chromatin (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C directly impacts nucleosome mobility and chromatin fiber motion in vitro.
source: Next, we find that the essential kinetochore protein CENP-C, which is CENP-A chromatin's closest binding partner, directly impacts nucleosome mobility and, surprisingly, also chromatin fiber motion in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the HS-AFM experiments in the introduction.

claim: Overexpressing CENP-C alters centromeric chromatin transcription and the ability to load new CENP-A molecules.
source: We extended these findings in vivo using immunofluorescence imaging and biochemical approaches, reporting that overexpressing CENP-C alters centromeric chromatin transcription and the ability to load new CENP-A molecules.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from in vivo experiments in the introduction.

claim: Local transcriptional competency depends on innate properties and local homeostasis of histone variants within the chromatin fiber in vivo.
source: Cumulatively, these data support the notion that local transcriptional competency depends on innate properties and local homeostasis of histone variants within the chromatin fiber in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cumulative data presented in the study.

claim: HS-AFM videos were obtained at a framerate of 0.5 Hz (2 s per frame) for a minimum of 20 s and up to 120 s.
source: Data acquisition: HS-AFM videos were obtained at a framerate of 0.5 Hz (2 s per frame) for a minimum of 20 s and up to 120 s.
evidence: Figure 1 describes the data acquisition parameters for HS-AFM.

claim: A total of 6052 individual nucleosome trajectories were obtained from 13 different samples.
source: Using MATLAB's single particle tracking MatlabTrack package, we obtained a total of 6052 individual nucleosome trajectories from 13 different samples (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Individual trajectories needed to be at least 20 s, with a maximum of 120 s (10–60 points) to obtain significant mean square displacement (MSD) values.
source: To obtain significant mean square displacement (MSD) values, individual trajectories needed to be of sufficient duration. Therefore, we selected individual trajectories that were at least 20 s, with a maximum of 120 s (10–60 points).
evidence: This describes a methodological criterion for data selection.

claim: The maximum single step size was estimated at twice the nucleosome width or 24 nm.
source: In addition, we wanted to make sure that we were tracking the same nucleosomes, so we estimated the maximum single step size at twice the nucleosome width or 24 nm.
evidence: This describes a methodological criterion for data selection.

claim: 3835 trajectories were analyzed to obtain the step angle, step size, mean square displacement (MSD), and diffusion constant of individual nucleosomes.
source: Finally, we analyzed 3835 trajectories to obtain the step angle, step size, mean square displacement (MSD), and diffusion constant of individual nucleosomes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: If the AFM tip altered samples during scanning, it would create a distinctive signature in single particle trajectories.
source: We reasoned that if the AFM tip altered samples during scanning, it would create a distinctive signature in single particle trajectories.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement used to design control experiments.

claim: No bias was observed in the angle distributions for CENP-A chromatin under multiple conditions.
source: We did not observe a bias in the angle distributions (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 2B and supplementary figures show the angle distributions for various conditions.

claim: Adding an excess of APS (333 nM APS is 2 x APS) lowers the diffusion constant compared to not adding APS (no APS).
source: We predicted that adding an excess of APS (333 nM APS is 2 x APS) would lower the diffusion constant compared to not adding APS (no APS). Indeed, we measured a lower diffusion constant for 2 x APS than no APS (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 2D shows the diffusion constants for different APS conditions.

claim: No bias was observed in the diffusion constants between the x-axis and y-axis for CENP-A chromatin.
source: If there were a tip effect, we reasoned there would be a difference in the diffusion constants between the x-axis and y-axis, which are parallel and perpendicular to the direction of tip scanning, respectively. We did not observe a bias in the diffusion constants between the two axes (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 2D and supplementary figures show the diffusion constants for x and y axes.

claim: No significant effect of video length on the step size was observed.
source: Third, to test for the potential impact of prolonged imaging on manipulation of trajectories, we assessed the step size distribution over time. We did not observe a significant effect of the video length on the step size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2), indicating that extended imaging did not alter the trajectory dynamics.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the step size distribution over time.

claim: HS-AFM does not introduce a tip effect on chromatin.
source: We are therefore confident that HS-AFM does not introduce a tip effect on chromatin and that drift is adequately corrected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments testing for tip effects.

claim: Different salt concentrations impact chromatin compaction and dynamics.
source: Different salt concentrations are known to impact chromatin compaction and dynamics (Allahverdi et al., 2015; Brasch et al., 1971; Yager et al., 1989; Yager and van Holde, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At lower salt concentrations (below 50 mM NaCl), nucleosomes are stabilized.
source: At lower salt concentrations (below 50 mM NaCl), nucleosomes are stabilized, whereas at higher salt concentrations (above 100 mM NaCl) nucleosomes become unstable.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about nucleosome behavior at different salt concentrations.

claim: At higher salt concentrations (above 100 mM NaCl) nucleosomes become unstable.
source: At lower salt concentrations (below 50 mM NaCl), nucleosomes are stabilized, whereas at higher salt concentrations (above 100 mM NaCl) nucleosomes become unstable.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about nucleosome behavior at different salt concentrations.

claim: 124 and 161 nucleosome trajectories were tracked for low salt and high salt conditions, respectively.
source: For each condition we tracked 124 and 161 nucleosome trajectories, respectively (Table 1, Figure 3—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Table 1 provides quantitative data on the number of trajectories tracked.

claim: The MSD curve for high salt had a larger slope than for low salt.
source: As expected, the MSD curve for high salt had a larger slope than for low salt (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3A shows the MSD curves for different salt conditions.

claim: The diffusion constant was 1.2±0.2 nm2·s–1 for low salt and 4.1±0.3 nm2·s–1 for high salt.
source: This is reflected in the diffusion constant, which was 1.2±0.2 nm2·s–1 for low salt and 4.1±0.3 nm2·s–1 for high salt (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3B and Table 1 provide the diffusion constants for different conditions.

claim: The average step size of CENP-A nucleosomes for high salt is double the length of that of low salt (5.5±0.2 nm vs 2.8±0.1 nm, respectively).
source: To better understand the step dynamics, we first assessed the average single-frame step size and found that the average step size of CENP-A nucleosomes for high salt is double the length of that of low salt (5.5±0.2 nm vs 2.8±0.1 nm, respectively, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C provide the average step sizes.

claim: The maximum R-step was 9.6±0.4 nm for low salt and 14.5±0.4 nm for high salt.
source: The maximum R-step was only slightly different between the low and high salt conditions (9.6±0.4 nm vs 14.5±0.4 nm, respectively, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D provide the maximum R-step values.

claim: The R-step range was 18.3±0.9 nm2 for low salt and 40±2 nm2 for high salt.
source: When we looked at the total range of a trajectory by calculating the R-step range, we observed a much larger variance in the distribution for the high salt compared to the low salt (40±2 nm2 vs 18.3±0.9 nm2, respectively, Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E provide the R-step range values.

claim: The x- and y- single-step distributions were poorly fit by single Gaussian distributions (D0), but were well-fit by a sum of two Gaussian distributions (D1 and D2).
source: Although the x- and y- single-step distributions were poorly fit by single Gaussian distributions (D0), they were well-fit by a sum of two Gaussian distributions (D1 and D2) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3D and supplementary figures show the Gaussian fitting of step distributions.

claim: The relative fraction of the two Gaussian distributions differed between low and high salt conditions.
source: The relative fraction of the two Gaussian distributions differed between low and high salt conditions (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3E shows the fractions of D1 and D2 Gaussian distributions.

claim: There are two distinct populations of nucleosomes in both low- and high-salt conditions.
source: These data indicate that there are two distinct populations of nucleosomes in both low- and high-salt conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gaussian fitting results.

claim: The D1 Gaussian population represents slower diffusing nucleosomes, potentially reflecting transient pausing.
source: The D1 Gaussian population represents slower diffusing nucleosomes, potentially reflecting transient pausing, whereas the D2 Gaussian population represents faster diffusing nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gaussian fitting results.

claim: The D2 Gaussian population represents faster diffusing nucleosomes.
source: The D1 Gaussian population represents slower diffusing nucleosomes, potentially reflecting transient pausing, whereas the D2 Gaussian population represents faster diffusing nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gaussian fitting results.

claim: Individual nucleosomes can switch from the smaller D1 diffusion constant to the larger D2 diffusion constant or vice versa.
source: To test for this possibility, we first manually verified whether individual nucleosomes could switch from what appears to be the smaller D1 diffusion constant to the larger D2 diffusion constant or vice versa. Indeed, we found a myriad of such examples across different conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 4A shows examples of nucleosomes switching between diffusion states.

claim: The effective diffusion constant of 'stuck' nucleosome trajectories was significantly smaller than that of the smaller diffusion constant from the fit of a sum of two Gaussians for most conditions.
source: With the exception of the 2 x APS and low-salt conditions, we found that the effective diffusion constant of the 'stuck' nucleosome trajectories was significantly smaller than that of the smaller diffusion constant from the fit of a sum of two Gaussians (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 5 shows the comparison of diffusion constants for stuck particles and D1.

claim: The data excludes the possibility of nucleosomes being 'stuck' to the mica surface.
source: In other words, these data would exclude the possibility of nucleosomes being 'stuck' to the mica surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of diffusion constants.

claim: Individual nucleosomes may have the capacity to move back and forth between the D1 and the D2 Gaussian distributions, indicating the possibility of switching between two diffusive modes.
source: Altogether, our data suggests that individual nucleosomes may have the capacity to move back and forth between the D1 and the D2 Gaussian distributions, indicating the possibility of switching between two diffusive modes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of nucleosome trajectories and Gaussian fitting.

claim: The average diffusion constant was higher in the absence of APS (7.5±0.5 nm2·s–1) than 2 x APS (2.5±0.3 nm2·s–1).
source: The average diffusion constant was also higher in the absence of APS (7.5±0.5 nm2·s–1) than 2 x APS (2.5±0.3 nm2·s–1, Figure 3B, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Figure 3B and Table 1 provide the diffusion constants for different APS conditions.

claim: CENP-A chromatin in the presence of Tween-20 behaved more like no APS and high salt conditions with a steep MSD curve, a very broad distribution of average step sizes, and a large R-step range distribution.
source: We found that CENP-A chromatin in the presence of Tween-20 behaved more like no APS and high salt conditions with a steep MSD curve, a very broad distribution of average step sizes, and a large R-step range distribution (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3 and supplementary figures show the MSD curves and step size distributions for Tween-20 condition.

claim: Tween-20 in the context of imaging CENP-A chromatin by HS-AFM primarily reduces non-specific hydrophobic interactions resulting in less restricted nucleosome mobility.
source: We interpret this to mean that Tween-20 in the context of imaging CENP-A chromatin by HS-AFM primarily reduces non-specific hydrophobic interactions resulting in less restricted nucleosome mobility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Tween-20 experimental results.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on the 8.5 kbp plasmid without known positioning sequences behaves similar to CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on 3.5 kbp plasmid with known positioning sequences.
source: Overall, it appears that CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on the 8.5 kbp plasmid without known positioning sequences behaves similar to CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on 3.5 kbp plasmid with known positioning sequences, thereby suggesting that nucleosome mobility measured in these experiments may be independent of DNA sequence specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing CENP-A nucleosomes on different plasmids.

claim: Nucleosome mobility measured in these experiments may be independent of DNA sequence specificity.
source: Overall, it appears that CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on the 8.5 kbp plasmid without known positioning sequences behaves similar to CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on 3.5 kbp plasmid with known positioning sequences, thereby suggesting that nucleosome mobility measured in these experiments may be independent of DNA sequence specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing CENP-A nucleosomes on different plasmids.

claim: A bias in both the angle between successive steps and Gaussian fitting of single step displacements was observed for H3 chromatin with or without linker histone H1.5 as well as H3 mononucleosomes.
source: When we analyzed previously published HS-AFM videos of H3 chromatin with or without linker histone H1.5 (Melters and Dalal, 2021) as well as H3 mononucleosomes, we observed a bias in both the angle between successive steps and Gaussian fitting of single step displacements (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7, Figure 3—videos 7–9, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7 show the analysis of H3 chromatin and mononucleosomes.

claim: Bias in HS-AFM trajectories is a possibility and can be detected.
source: These data provide evidence that bias in HS-AFM trajectories is a possibility and that it can be detected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of H3 chromatin and mononucleosomes.

claim: There was no difference in fitting either a single or double Gaussian distributions for H3 mononucleosomes.
source: Furthermore, there was no difference in fitting either a single or double Gaussian distributions for H3 mononucleosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 7F).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 7F shows the Gaussian fitting for H3 mononucleosomes.

claim: The diffusion constant of mononucleosomes is about threefold larger than that of chromatin arrays.
source: We observed that the diffusion constant of mononucleosomes is about threefold larger than that of chromatin arrays (Table 1) and 10- to 185-fold larger than the D1 diffusion constants observed under various conditions (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 7).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 7 provide the diffusion constants for mononucleosomes and chromatin arrays.

claim: The R-step range of mononucleosomes is roughly twofold larger than chromatin arrays.
source: In addition, the R-step range of mononucleosomes is roughly twofold larger than chromatin arrays (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 provides the R-step range values for mononucleosomes and chromatin arrays.

claim: The unconstrained motion of mononucleosomes results in a single Gaussian distribution of step displacements.
source: Therefore, the latter observations imply that the unconstrained motion of mononucleosomes results in a single Gaussian distribution of step displacements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of mononucleosome dynamics.

claim: CENP-A chromatin responded to varying salt and APS concentrations in agreement with previous reports.
source: Altogether, when we analyzed HS-AFM videos, CENP-A chromatin responded to varying salt and APS concentrations in agreement with previous reports (Allahverdi et al., 2015; Brasch et al., 1971; Lyubchenko et al., 2014; Shlyakhtenko et al., 2003; Yager et al., 1989; Yager and van Holde, 1984).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations to previous literature and the data presented.

claim: Low salt and 2 x APS concentrations reduced CENP-A nucleosome mobility.
source: Low salt and 2 x APS concentrations reduced CENP-A nucleosome mobility, whereas high salt and no APS concentrations increased CENP-A nucleosome mobility (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 8 summarizes the effects of different conditions on CENP-A nucleosome mobility.

claim: High salt and no APS concentrations increased CENP-A nucleosome mobility.
source: Low salt and 2 x APS concentrations reduced CENP-A nucleosome mobility, whereas high salt and no APS concentrations increased CENP-A nucleosome mobility (Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 8 summarizes the effects of different conditions on CENP-A nucleosome mobility.

claim: CENP-CCD rigidified CENP-A nucleosomes and induced CENP-A nucleosome clustering.
source: Previously, we showed that a central domain fragment of CENP-C (Figure 4A) rigidified CENP-A nucleosomes and induced CENP-A nucleosome clustering (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding by the authors.

claim: CENP-CCD would reduce CENP-A nucleosome mobility.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesized that CENP-CCD would reduce CENP-A nucleosome mobility.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: 498, 368, 310, and 166 trajectories were obtained for CENP-A alone, 1x, 2x, and 4x CENP-CCD, respectively.
source: From at least 3 experiments per sample, we obtained 498, 368, 310, and 166 trajectories, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 provides the number of trajectories for each condition.

claim: Individual MSD curves of CENP-A nucleosomes were broadly distributed.
source: Next, we calculated the MSD of CENP-A nucleosomes alone or in the presence of 1 x, 2 x, or 4 x CENP-CCD and found that individual MSD curves of CENP-A nucleosomes were broadly distributed (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B), with an average MSD curve that reached a plateau after ~25 s (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), implying confined motion (Kapanidis et al., 2018; Zhong and Wang, 2020).
evidence: Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A show the MSD curves for CENP-A nucleosomes with and without CENP-CCD.

claim: The average MSD curve of CENP-A nucleosomes reached a plateau after ~25 s, implying confined motion.
source: Next, we calculated the MSD of CENP-A nucleosomes alone or in the presence of 1 x, 2 x, or 4 x CENP-CCD and found that individual MSD curves of CENP-A nucleosomes were broadly distributed (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B), with an average MSD curve that reached a plateau after ~25 s (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), implying confined motion (Kapanidis et al., 2018; Zhong and Wang, 2020).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2A shows the average MSD curve reaching a plateau.

claim: When CENP-CCD was added at either 2 x or 4 x molar excess to CENP-A nucleosomes, CENP-A nucleosome mobility was strongly restricted.
source: When CENP-CCD was added at either 2 x or 4 x molar excess to CENP-A nucleosomes, CENP-A nucleosome mobility was strongly restricted (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Figure 4—videos 2–4, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A show the MSD curves for CENP-A nucleosomes with 2x and 4x CENP-CCD.

claim: The MSD curve was much lower for 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD compared to CENP-A alone.
source: Indeed, the MSD curve was much lower for 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD compared to CENP-A alone, and the 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD MSD curve maintained a shallow slope (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A show the MSD curves for different CENP-CCD concentrations.

claim: The 1 x CENP-CCD MSD curve was similar to CENP-A alone.
source: In contrast, the 1 x CENP-CCD MSD curve was similar to CENP-A alone (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B show the MSD curves for 1x CENP-CCD.

claim: The diffusion constant of CENP-A alone was 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1.
source: The diffusion constant of CENP-A alone was 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1, whereas the addition of 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD reduced the diffusion constant 2.9-fold to 0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1 and 3.8-fold to 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1, respectively (Table 1, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 4E provide the diffusion constants for CENP-A alone and with CENP-CCD.

claim: The addition of 2 x CENP-CCD reduced the diffusion constant 2.9-fold to 0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1.
source: The diffusion constant of CENP-A alone was 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1, whereas the addition of 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD reduced the diffusion constant 2.9-fold to 0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1 and 3.8-fold to 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1, respectively (Table 1, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 4E provide the diffusion constants for CENP-A with 2x CENP-CCD.

claim: The addition of 4 x CENP-CCD reduced the diffusion constant 3.8-fold to 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1.
source: The diffusion constant of CENP-A alone was 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1, whereas the addition of 2 x and 4 x CENP-CCD reduced the diffusion constant 2.9-fold to 0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1 and 3.8-fold to 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1, respectively (Table 1, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Table 1 and Figure 4E provide the diffusion constants for CENP-A with 4x CENP-CCD.

claim: CENP-CCD restricts CENP-A nucleosome mobility in a switch-like manner.
source: Overall, by HS-AFM we observed that CENP-CCD restricts CENP-A nucleosome mobility in a switch-like manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HS-AFM experiments with CENP-CCD.

claim: This switch could be the mechanism by which overexpression of CENP-C in living cells results in CENP-A chromatin clustering.
source: We hypothesized that this switch, as we recently observed (Melters et al., 2019), could be the mechanism by which overexpression of CENP-C in living cells results in CENP-A chromatin clustering.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Overexpressing CENP-C in HeLa cells resulted in increased clustering of centromeric chromatin and loss of centromeric RNAP2.
source: Previously, we showed that overexpressing CENP-C in HeLa cells resulted in increased clustering of centromeric chromatin and loss of centromeric RNAP2 (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding by the authors.

claim: Centromeric non-coding α-satellite transcription might be impaired in the background of CENP-C overexpression.
source: These results, combined with our 'decrease of motion' observations above, suggest that centromeric non-coding α-satellite transcription might be impaired in the background of CENP-C overexpression.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the combined results from HS-AFM and previous findings.

claim: CENP-C was overexpressed 2.8-fold in HeLa cells.
source: We overexpressed CENP-C 2.8-fold (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2) in HeLa cells for 72 hr and subsequently purified CENP-A chromatin associated with CENP-C by CENP-C native ChIP (nChIP), and the unbound CENP-A chromatin was pulled-down by sequential ACA nChIP.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows the level of CENP-C overexpression.

claim: RNAP2 levels were reduced upon CENP-C overexpression.
source: We found that RNAP2 levels were reduced upon CENP-C overexpression (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 5A shows the quantification of RNAP2 levels with CENP-C overexpression.

claim: Total CENP-A levels were reduced upon CENP-C overexpression.
source: In addition, we observed that, upon CENP-C overexpression, total CENP-A levels were also reduced (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Figure 5B shows the quantification of CENP-A levels with CENP-C overexpression.

claim: A ~60% reduction in α-satellite transcripts was observed in cells overexpressing CENP-C.
source: By quantitative PCR, we observed a ~60% reduction in α-satellite transcripts in cells overexpressing CENP-C (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 5C shows the quantification of α-satellite transcription with CENP-C overexpression.

claim: CENP-A levels are reduced and centromeric transcription is impaired upon CENP-C overexpression.
source: These results indicate that CENP-A levels are reduced and that centromeric transcription is indeed impaired upon CENP-C overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nChIP and qPCR experiments.

claim: New CENP-A loading is transcriptionally regulated.
source: Previous reports showed that new CENP-A loading is transcriptionally regulated (Jansen et al., 2007; Quénet and Dalal, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-C overexpression leads to defective de novo CENP-A loading.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that CENP-C overexpression leads to defective de novo CENP-A loading.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on previous reports and their findings.

claim: A 1.3-fold reduction of de novo incorporation of CENP-A was observed in a CENP-C overexpression background.
source: Strikingly, in an CENP-C overexpression background, we observed a 1.3-fold reduction of de novo incorporation of CENP-A (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 6C and D show the quantification of de novo CENP-A loading with CENP-C overexpression.

claim: The functional consequences of CENP-C overexpression are suppression of α-satellite transcription and subsequent impairment of new CENP-A loading.
source: Thus, the functional consequences of CENP-C overexpression are suppression of α-satellite transcription (Figure 5C) and subsequent impairment of new CENP-A loading (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the in vivo findings.

claim: The AFM tip scanning motion does not generate observable artifacts in nucleosome dynamics.
source: Importantly, we show that the AFM tip scanning motion does not generate observable artifacts in nucleosome dynamics (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Salt dialysis is a common method for in vitro nucleosome reconstitution.
source: Case in point, salt dialysis is a common method for in vitro nucleosome reconstitution (Cruz-Becerra and Kadonaga, 2021; Peterson, 2008; Walkiewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low salt restricted CENP-A nucleosome motion, whereas high salt did the opposite.
source: Indeed, low salt restricted CENP-A nucleosome motion, whereas high salt did the opposite (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the salt concentration experiments.

claim: Not functionalizing the mica surface resulted in more mobile CENP-A nucleosomes.
source: Not functionalizing the mica surface resulted in more mobile CENP-A nucleosomes, whereas 2 x APS functionalized mica resulted in increased levels of immobile CENP-A nucleosomes (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the APS experiments.

claim: 2 x APS functionalized mica resulted in increased levels of immobile CENP-A nucleosomes.
source: Not functionalizing the mica surface resulted in more mobile CENP-A nucleosomes, whereas 2 x APS functionalized mica resulted in increased levels of immobile CENP-A nucleosomes (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the APS experiments.

claim: The diffusion constant for CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on PCAT2 containing plasmid was higher than that of CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on α-satellite containing plasmid imaged under the same conditions.
source: Interestingly, the diffusion constant for CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on PCAT2 containing plasmid was higher than that of CENP-A nucleosomes reconstituted on α-satellite containing plasmid imaged under the same conditions (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 provides the diffusion constants for CENP-A nucleosomes on different plasmids.

claim: H3 mononucleosomes were the only nucleosomes for which the single-frame step size distribution was well-fit by a single Gaussian.
source: In addition, H3 mononucleosomes were the only nucleosomes for which the single-frame step size distribution was well-fit by a single Gaussian (Figure 3—figure supplement 7F), this is in stark contrast with CENP-A chromatin, for which the step size distribution is well-fit by the sum of two Gaussians (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 7F shows the Gaussian fitting for H3 mononucleosomes.

claim: Nucleosome arrays might drive the two mobility states observed.
source: This implies that nucleosome arrays might drive the two mobility states we observed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of mononucleosomes and chromatin arrays.

claim: Nucleosomes can switch between the D1 and D2 state.
source: Looking more closely at individual tracks, we noticed that nucleosomes can switch between the D1 and D2 state (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 3 shows examples of nucleosomes switching between diffusion states.

claim: The slower D1 diffusion constant did not appear to simply reflect nucleosomes being stuck to the mica surface.
source: The slower D1 diffusion constant did not appear to simply reflect nucleosomes being stuck to the mica surface (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 5 shows the comparison of D1 diffusion constant with stuck particles.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes respond to various control conditions in a predictable manner.
source: Altogether, these data provide evidence that CENP-A nucleosomes respond to various control conditions in a predictable manner, but also that their dynamics are complex and include at least two mobility states.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the control experiments.

claim: CENP-A nucleosome dynamics are complex and include at least two mobility states.
source: Altogether, these data provide evidence that CENP-A nucleosomes respond to various control conditions in a predictable manner, but also that their dynamics are complex and include at least two mobility states.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the control experiments.

claim: CENP-C modulates both CENP-A nucleosome accessibility and its elasticity.
source: CENP-C modulates both CENP-A nucleosome accessibility (Ali-Ahmad et al., 2019; Ariyoshi et al., 2021; Falk et al., 2016; Falk et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017) and its elasticity (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-CCD regulates CENP-A nucleosomes mobility in a switch-like manner.
source: Here, we show that CENP-CCD regulates CENP-A nucleosomes mobility in a switch-like manner (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the CENP-CCD experiments.

claim: CENP-C compacts CENP-A chromatin once a critical mass is reached.
source: This might imply that CENP-C compacts CENP-A chromatin once a critical mass is reached.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the switch-like behavior observed with CENP-CCD.

claim: The data presented correlates with CENP-CCD rigidification of CENP-A nucleosomes.
source: The data presented here correlates with CENP-CCD rigidification of CENP-A nucleosomes (Melters et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement connecting the current findings with previous work.

claim: In vivo, CENP-C overexpression results in reduced levels of centromeric RNAP2, impaired centromeric transcription, and decreased loading of new CENP-A at the centromere.
source: Additionally, we show that in vivo, CENP-C overexpression results in reduced levels of centromeric RNAP2 (Melters et al., 2019), impaired centromeric transcription (Figure 5C), and subsequent decreased loading of new CENP-A at the centromere (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo findings.

claim: These findings combined provide evidence for a speculative link between the physical properties of nucleosomes, their mobility along DNA, and how these material properties might regulate chromatin accessibility and transcriptional potential.
source: These findings combined provide evidence for a speculative link between the physical properties of nucleosomes, their mobility along DNA, and how these material properties might regulate chromatin accessibility and transcriptional potential.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: Nucleosomes within heterochromatin were less dynamic compared to euchromatin regions.
source: Nucleosomes within heterochromatin were less dynamic compared to euchromatin regions (Ashwin et al., 2019; Maeshima et al., 2023; Nozaki et al., 2017; Ricci et al., 2015), transcriptional inhibition diminished constraints of local chromatin movements (Nagashima et al., 2019), and local levels of H1 correlated with reduced nucleosome dynamics (Gómez-García et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transcriptional inhibition diminished constraints of local chromatin movements.
source: Nucleosomes within heterochromatin were less dynamic compared to euchromatin regions (Ashwin et al., 2019; Maeshima et al., 2023; Nozaki et al., 2017; Ricci et al., 2015), transcriptional inhibition diminished constraints of local chromatin movements (Nagashima et al., 2019), and local levels of H1 correlated with reduced nucleosome dynamics (Gómez-García et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Local levels of H1 correlated with reduced nucleosome dynamics.
source: Nucleosomes within heterochromatin were less dynamic compared to euchromatin regions (Ashwin et al., 2019; Maeshima et al., 2023; Nozaki et al., 2017; Ricci et al., 2015), transcriptional inhibition diminished constraints of local chromatin movements (Nagashima et al., 2019), and local levels of H1 correlated with reduced nucleosome dynamics (Gómez-García et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chromatin-associated H1-eGFP mobility was two orders of magnitude smaller than free H1-eGFP.
source: Indeed, chromatin-associated H1-eGFP mobility was two orders of magnitude smaller than free H1-eGFP (Bernas et al., 2014; Wachsmuth et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GFP-tagged loci in CHO cells showed a slow and fast diffusion coefficient of 0.24·10–3 and 3.13·10–3 µm2·s–1.
source: Using fluorescence recovery spectroscopy, GFP-tagged loci in CHO cells showed a slow and fast diffusion coefficient of 0.24·10–3 and 3.13·10–3 µm2·s–1 (Levi et al., 2005) and TetO tagged-DNA DHJH loci in B cells had a diffusion coefficient of ~2.0·103 µm2·s0.5 (Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TetO tagged-DNA DHJH loci in B cells had a diffusion coefficient of ~2.0·103 µm2·s0.5.
source: Using fluorescence recovery spectroscopy, GFP-tagged loci in CHO cells showed a slow and fast diffusion coefficient of 0.24·10–3 and 3.13·10–3 µm2·s–1 (Levi et al., 2005) and TetO tagged-DNA DHJH loci in B cells had a diffusion coefficient of ~2.0·103 µm2·s0.5 (Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The change in diffusion coefficient of VHDH loci results in a fourfold increase in interaction frequency.
source: The change in diffusion coefficient of VHDH loci is interpreted to results in a fourfold increase in interaction frequency (Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The diffusion constant of H3 mononucleosomes sliding along a DNA strand is ~1.3 bp2·s–1 (~0.15 nm2·s–1).
source: A recent study using optical tweezers showed that the diffusion constant of H3 mononucleosomes sliding along a DNA strand is ~1.3 bp2·s–1 (~0.15 nm2·s–1; Rudnizky et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The D1 diffusion constant might reflect sliding nucleosomes.
source: This value is roughly similar to the D1 diffusion constants we observed (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 7, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2), implying that the D1 diffusion constant might reflect sliding nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing the current findings with previous literature.

claim: Binding of transcription factors to nucleosomal DNA biases nucleosome motion, potentially through manipulation of the folding and unfolding of nucleosomal DNA around the nucleosome core particle.
source: Binding of transcription factors to nucleosomal DNA biases nucleosome motion, potentially through manipulation of the folding and unfolding of nucleosomal DNA around the nucleosome core particle (Donovan et al., 2023; Rudnizky et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes have an average diffusion constant of 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1.
source: Here, we show that CENP-A nucleosomes have an average diffusion constant of 2.3±0.2 nm2·s–1 and their single-step distribution was well-fit by a sum of two Gaussian distributions (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for CENP-A nucleosomes.

claim: When CENP-CCD was added at a two- or fourfold molar ratio to CENP-A nucleosomes, a diffusion constant of about three times lower than CENP-A nucleosomes alone was observed (0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1 and 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1, respectively).
source: When CENP-CCD was added at a two- or fourfold molar ratio to CENP-A nucleosomes, we observed a diffusion constant that is about three times lower than CENP-A nucleosomes alone (0.78±0.06 nm2·s–1 and 0.61±0.05 nm2·s–1, respectively).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for CENP-A nucleosomes with CENP-CCD.

claim: The difference in diffusion constants for nucleosomes between the Rudnizky study (~0.15 nm2·s–1) and the current results (0.61–2.3 nm2·s–1) could be due to technical differences of their experimental set-up compared to the current experimental approach (optical tweezers vs HS-AFM).
source: This difference in diffusion constants for nucleosomes between the Rudnizky study (~0.15 nm2·s–1, [Rudnizky et al., 2019]) and our results (0.61–2.3 nm2·s–1) could be due to technical differences of their experimental set-up compared to our experimental approach (optical tweezers vs HS-AFM).
evidence: This is a discussion of potential reasons for differences in diffusion constants.

claim: Nucleosome arrays permit both one-dimensional (nucleosome sliding) and two-dimensional motions (whole chromatin fiber movement) of nucleosomes compared to mononucleosomes that were fixed to polystyrene beads, which only permit one-dimensional motion.
source: We used nucleosome arrays which permit both one-dimensional (nucleosome sliding) and two-dimensional motions (whole chromatin fiber movement) of nucleosomes compared to mononucleosomes that were fixed to polystyrene beads, which only permit one-dimensional motion (Rudnizky et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a discussion of the differences between the current experimental approach and previous studies.

claim: Calculated diffusion constants for H2B-eGFP range from 0.0019 µm2·s–1 to 7.3 µm2·s–1.
source: Calculated diffusion constants for H2B-eGFP range from 0.0019 µm2·s–1 to 7.3 µm2·s–1 (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Mazza et al., 2012) and 0.03 µm2·s–1 to 1.39 µm2·s–1 for HALO-H2B (Lovely et al., 2020; Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Calculated diffusion constants for HALO-H2B range from 0.03 µm2·s–1 to 1.39 µm2·s–1.
source: Calculated diffusion constants for H2B-eGFP range from 0.0019 µm2·s–1 to 7.3 µm2·s–1 (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Mazza et al., 2012) and 0.03 µm2·s–1 to 1.39 µm2·s–1 for HALO-H2B (Lovely et al., 2020; Ranjan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vivo H2B diffusion constants are several orders of magnitudes larger than observed in the current study (0.61–2.3 nm2·s–1).
source: These in vivo H2B diffusion constants are several orders of magnitudes larger than we observed (0.61–2.3 nm2·s–1).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with in vivo studies.

claim: The difference in diffusion constants between in vivo and in vitro could be due to the many activities within the nucleus of a living cell compared to the steady-state nature of an in vitro experiment.
source: This could be due to the many activities within the nucleus of a living cell compared to the steady-state nature of an in vitro experiment.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential reasons for differences in diffusion constants.

claim: The potential of single molecule analysis by HS-AFM to contribute to elegant studies in the field is exciting, as it can link single-molecule force spectroscopy analysis to in vivo single molecule tracking experiments.
source: As such, the potential of single molecule analysis by HS-AFM to contribute to elegant studies in the field is exciting, as it can link single-molecule force spectroscopy analysis to in vivo single molecule tracking experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the current work.

claim: The diffusion constant of H2A.Z nucleosomes is larger than H3 nucleosomes.
source: Looking at another histone variant nucleosome, the diffusion constant of H2A.Z nucleosomes is larger than H3 nucleosomes (Rudnizky et al., 2019), which correlates with the transcriptional buffering function of H2A.Z (Chen et al., 2019; Giaimo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The larger diffusion constant of H2A.Z nucleosomes correlates with the transcriptional buffering function of H2A.Z.
source: Looking at another histone variant nucleosome, the diffusion constant of H2A.Z nucleosomes is larger than H3 nucleosomes (Rudnizky et al., 2019), which correlates with the transcriptional buffering function of H2A.Z (Chen et al., 2019; Giaimo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transcription through CENP-A chromatin would be more efficient compared to H3 chromatin.
source: A logical prediction from our results would be that transcription through CENP-A chromatin would be more efficient compared to H3 chromatin.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings.

claim: CENP-A creates an open chromatin structure.
source: Indeed, a recent single-molecule study showed that CENP-A creates an open chromatin structure (Nagpal and Fierz, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Proteins that exert their activity by binding to the outer surface of nucleosomes, rather than changing the internal constituents of nucleosomes, have the opposite effect on transcription.
source: We found that proteins that exert their activity by binding to the outer surface of nucleosomes, rather than changing the internal constituents of nucleosomes, have the opposite effect on transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: CENP-CCD-CENP-A nucleosomes have a significantly reduced diffusion constant compared to CENP-A nucleosomes alone.
source: CENP-CCD rigidifies CENP-A nucleosomes (Melters et al., 2019), and CENP-CCD-CENP-A nucleosomes have a significantly reduced diffusion constant compared to CENP-A nucleosomes alone (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for CENP-CCD-CENP-A nucleosomes.

claim: Overexpression of CENP-C resulted in decreased centromeric transcription.
source: In vivo, overexpression of CENP-C resulted in decreased centromeric transcription (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo findings.

claim: Nucleosome dynamics are highly tunable, with tuners that can dampen or exaggerate nucleosome motion, which correlates with higher order chromatin folding and accessibility.
source: Thus, this study significantly extends the existing paradigm that suggests nucleosome dynamics are highly tunable, with a surprising twist – tuners can dampen or exaggerate nucleosome motion, which correlates with higher order chromatin folding and accessibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: Chromatin effector partners modify the material properties of histone variant nucleosomes at the local level, supporting the formation of functional nucleosome clutches.
source: Taking these and prior findings in context, our data suggest a model where chromatin effector partners modify the material properties of histone variant nucleosomes at the local level, supporting the formation of functional nucleosome clutches (Portillo-Ledesma et al., 2021; Ricci et al., 2015; Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: CENP-A nucleosomes recruit CENP-C to form a kinetochore-promoting CENP-A chromatin clutch.
source: CENP-A nucleosomes recruit CENP-C to form a kinetochore-promoting CENP-A chromatin clutch (Kale et al., 2023).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model and is supported by a citation.

claim: CENP-C functions as the template for the recruitment of additional kinetochore proteins.
source: CENP-C functions as the template for the recruitment of additional kinetochore proteins (Klare et al., 2015; Yatskevich et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When CENP-C binds, CENP-A nucleosomes become rigidified and restrict CENP-A nucleosomes mobility.
source: When CENP-C binds, CENP-A nucleosomes become rigidified (Melters et al., 2019) and restrict CENP-A nucleosomes mobility (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for CENP-C binding to CENP-A nucleosomes.

claim: This unique clutch facilitates the recruitment of other inner kinetochore components by locally immobilizing CENP-A chromatin.
source: This unique clutch facilitates the recruitment of other inner kinetochore components by locally immobilizing CENP-A chromatin (Yatskevich et al., 2023).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model and is supported by a citation.

claim: To load new CENP-A molecules, transcription must happen.
source: Yet, to load new CENP-A molecules, transcription must happen (Arunkumar and Melters, 2020; Quénet and Dalal, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The repressive chromatin state that CENP-C induces contradicts the functional necessity of transcription for loading new CENP-A molecules.
source: The repressive chromatin state that CENP-C induces (Figure 5) contradicts this functional necessity.
evidence: This is a statement about the apparent contradiction between CENP-C's effects and the need for transcription.

claim: Cells can work around the juxtaposition of the dual functions of CENP-A chromatin by maintaining a pool of free centromeric CENP-A nucleosomes.
source: One speculative manner in which cells can work around the juxtaposition of the dual functions of CENP-A chromatin is by maintaining a pool of free centromeric CENP-A nucleosomes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how cells might resolve the contradiction.

claim: Centromeric CENP-C levels are lower compared to CENP-A levels.
source: Indeed, ChIP-seq and FISH data have established that centromeric CENP-C levels are lower compared to CENP-A levels (Henikoff et al., 2015; Kyriacou and Heun, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Unbound elastic and mobile CENP-A chromatin clutches create an intrinsically accessible chromatin state, allowing for the recruitment of transcriptional machinery that maintains centromeric CENP-A levels to facilitate both opposing functions.
source: We propose that unbound elastic and mobile CENP-A chromatin clutches create an intrinsically accessible chromatin state, allowing for the recruitment of transcriptional machinery that maintains centromeric CENP-A levels to facilitate both opposing functions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: The epigenetic fate of a locus may be tightly, possibly causally, linked to the mechanical state of the chromatin fiber.
source: Succinctly, the epigenetic fate of a locus may be tightly, possibly causally, linked to the mechanical state of the chromatin fiber; concomitantly, the reinstatement of an epigenetic signature by de novo loading of a particular variant, reinforces the mechanical state of the fiber.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: The reinstatement of an epigenetic signature by de novo loading of a particular variant, reinforces the mechanical state of the fiber.
source: Succinctly, the epigenetic fate of a locus may be tightly, possibly causally, linked to the mechanical state of the chromatin fiber; concomitantly, the reinstatement of an epigenetic signature by de novo loading of a particular variant, reinforces the mechanical state of the fiber.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the current findings.

claim: MSDs and diffusion constants for CENP-A nucleosomes under a variety of conditions are reported.
source: In summary, we report the MSDs and diffusion constants for CENP-A nucleosomes under a variety of conditions, and we show that single-step distributions are well-fit by the sum of two Gaussians.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Single-step distributions are well-fit by the sum of two Gaussians.
source: In summary, we report the MSDs and diffusion constants for CENP-A nucleosomes under a variety of conditions, and we show that single-step distributions are well-fit by the sum of two Gaussians.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Nucleosomes exist in at least two distinct mobility states.
source: This implies that nucleosomes exist in at least two distinct mobility states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Gaussian fitting results.

claim: CENP-C limits CENP-A mobility once a critical concentration is reached.
source: As we observed a switch-like behavior of restricting CENP-A nucleosome motions, instead of a linear dose-response, we speculate that CENP-C limits CENP-A mobility once a critical concentration is reached.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the switch-like behavior observed.

claim: Diminished transcriptional competence was observed when CENP-C is overexpressed, resulting in suppression of de novo CENP-A loading.
source: In vivo, we observed diminished transcriptional competence when CENP-C is overexpressed, resulting in suppression of de novo CENP-A loading.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo findings.

claim: There is a mechanistic link between modulating the material properties of nucleosomes and chromatin accessibility.
source: These results strongly imply that there is a mechanistic link between modulating the material properties of nucleosomes and chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: Nucleosome dynamics play an important role in genome compaction and regulating DNA access by DNA binding factors.
source: Nucleosome dynamics play an important role in genome compaction and regulating DNA access by DNA binding factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Nucleosome dynamics are driven by only a few interactions between the interfaces of DNA and nucleosomes.
source: These dynamics are driven by only a few interactions between the interfaces of DNA and nucleosomes (Fierz and Poirier, 2019; Polach and Widom, 1995; Widom, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.
